demos.title: Connect the on-premises/edge machines to Azure Arc
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: a Windows server in our own datacenter gets the Azure Connected Machine agent and becomes a resource in Azure, with one outbound connection and no inbound ports or VPN. We prove it worked from both sides, on the machine and in Azure, because an installer that exits cleanly is not proof. Connecting only makes the server manageable; monitoring, security and Policy are separate steps shown later in the session.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: cas26-arcwin01 is the presenter's on-premises Windows Server virtual machine (the demo target); MGMT-RAL-HV-01 is the standalone Hyper-V host it runs on; rg-tplabs-cas26-ops-eus-01 is the Azure resource group it lands in (the 'operations resource group'); Event=cas26 is the tag the lab puts on its own machines. To reproduce, substitute your own server, subscription and resource group.

To reproduce: a supported Windows Server with outbound HTTPS (443) to the Azure Arc endpoints, local administrator rights on it, an Azure identity allowed to onboard servers into <your-resource-group> (for example the Azure Connected Machine Onboarding role), and Azure CLI plus PowerShell 7 on your workstation.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: shared/foundation/config/variables.yml drives Connect-Cas26Arc.ps1, independently of demo.local.json. Confirm on_prem.windows_guest.name=cas26-arcwin01, cluster_node=MGMT-RAL-HV-01 (by exact IP, with its local credential), cluster_role=false, and the tenant, subscription and operations resource group, before any installation.

Presenter lab: cas26-arcwin01 is booted, network-attached and reachable from the presenter jump; its local administrator credential is in the CAS26 Key Vault; the Arc endpoints resolve and are reachable outbound; the agent package is pre-staged. Edge means connected edge: no disconnected-management promise.

Presenter lab: the guest lands in rg-tplabs-cas26-ops-eus-01 with Event=cas26 and no Owner tag; the Policy demo (slide 42) depends on that missing tag. If it is still connected from rehearsal, the helper reports the existing resource and the demo inspects it; never disconnect a working shared machine to restage. The Linux guest cas26-lnx01 runs on the SCVMM cluster and was brought into Arc through SCVMM (slides 9-11), not by this demo.
demos.reset: Keep the Arc connection: the Sentinel, Policy and Update Manager demos use this machine. Never disconnect and reconnect a shared machine between sessions; tearing down the lab after the event is a separate reviewed procedure.
demos.fallback: If installation or the portal is slow, show the rehearsal capture that pairs azcmagent show output with the matching Azure resource ID, and say which step you would have run.
demos.wait: Agent installation and connection run asynchronously, and the Azure view can lag the agent by a minute. Pre-stage the agent package and keep the rehearsal capture ready instead of polling on stage.

steps.title: Show which Azure account and which machine we are using
steps.body: In the presenter terminal (PowerShell 7, repository root), run the two lines below. The first loads the demo identifiers into $Demo and refuses to continue if the signed-in tenant or subscription differs from the configuration; the second prints the signed-in account. Then say which machine we connect (cas26-arcwin01) and where it runs (Hyper-V host MGMT-RAL-HV-01 in our datacenter).
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
az account show --query '{tenant:tenantId,subscription:id,name:name,user:user.name}' -o json
steps.expected: 'Demo configuration validated (current Azure context)', then a JSON block whose tenant and subscription match demo.local.json and whose user is the presenter's onboarding identity.
steps.troubleshooting: A tenant/subscription mismatch is a stop: run az account set --subscription <workload subscription> (the jump defaults to the management subscription) and rerun. If it asks you to populate a field, fix demo.local.json. Never carry on under a different account.
steps.speaker: Say: before we touch anything, this is the Azure account we are using and this is the one server we are connecting, a Windows VM on a Hyper-V host in our own datacenter.
steps.attendee: Confirm the tenant, subscription and target machine before onboarding; the common mistake is the right machine landing in the wrong place.

steps.title: Preview what the onboarding script will do
steps.body: Run the preview. Connect-Cas26Arc.ps1 is the lab's wrapper around standard Arc onboarding: it opens a session on the guest, installs the Azure Connected Machine agent and runs azcmagent connect. -DryRun prints the target and settings without changing anything. Point at three things in the output: the guest name, the resource group and the Event=cas26 tag.
steps.code:
pwsh ./shared/foundation/scripts/Connect-Cas26Arc.ps1 -Target Windows -DryRun
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'The operation failed. Stop and follow the recovery instructions.' }
steps.expected: The preview names only cas26-arcwin01, the operations resource group and the Event=cas26 tag; it asks for no cluster node or Linux address. Nothing is installed.
steps.troubleshooting: If the preview names another guest, resource group or subscription, stop: fix shared/foundation/config/variables.yml and rerun the preview. If it throws, read the error aloud and switch to the rehearsal capture; do not run step 3 against an unverified target.
steps.speaker: Say: this does what the portal's 'Add a server' script does: install one agent, make one outbound connection. The preview shows where it will land, and that resource group decides which access and Policy rules it inherits.
steps.attendee: Where a server lands (subscription and resource group) decides which rules it inherits, so check it before connecting.

steps.title: Connect the server
steps.body: Run the same command without -DryRun. It installs the agent if needed and connects the guest. If the guest is still connected from rehearsal, the script reports the existing resource instead of reconnecting; that is fine, carry on. Never show access tokens, credentials or temporary token files on screen.
steps.code:
pwsh ./shared/foundation/scripts/Connect-Cas26Arc.ps1 -Target Windows
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'The operation failed. Stop and follow the recovery instructions.' }
steps.expected: The script finishes without an error and reports the Arc resource for cas26-arcwin01, newly connected or already connected.
steps.troubleshooting: If sign-in, outbound access to the Arc endpoints or the package install fails, keep the error on screen, say which one failed and show the rehearsal capture. Do not rerun against another target and never disconnect another Arc machine to retry.
steps.speaker: Say: one outbound connection on port 443, no inbound ports, no VPN. The application on this server never uses this connection.
steps.attendee: Arc onboarding is one agent and one outbound HTTPS connection; the workload itself is untouched.

steps.title: Check the agent on the server itself
steps.body: Switch to the administrative PowerShell session on cas26-arcwin01 (RDP or a remote session from the jump) and run azcmagent show. Read out the resource name, resource group, subscription, tenant and Agent Status.
steps.code: azcmagent show
steps.expected: Agent Status: Connected, with resource name cas26-arcwin01, the operations resource group and the same tenant and subscription as step 1. A successful installer exit alone is not enough.
steps.troubleshooting: If azcmagent is not recognised, run it by full path: & 'C:\Program Files\AzureConnectedMachineAgent\azcmagent.exe' show. If the status is Disconnected, run azcmagent check on the guest to test the endpoints, then show the rehearsal capture. The portal alone cannot prove which machine's agent is connected.
steps.speaker: Say: proof has two sides. This is the machine's side: the agent says it is connected, and to which Azure resource.
steps.attendee: Check the agent on the machine (azcmagent show) as well as the portal; an installer that exits cleanly is not proof.

steps.title: Check the same machine in Azure
steps.body: Back in the presenter terminal, run the command. Compare the resource ID with what azcmagent show printed, then point at the system-assigned managed identity (the machine's own identity in Microsoft Entra ID, used later by extensions) and the tags.
steps.code: az resource show --ids $Demo.OnPremArcResourceId --query '{id:id,type:type,location:location,identity:identity,tags:tags,properties:properties}' -o json
steps.expected: One Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines resource named cas26-arcwin01 in the operations resource group, identity type SystemAssigned, status Connected, and tags that include Event=cas26 but no Owner tag.
steps.troubleshooting: The Azure view can lag the agent by a minute; rerun once. A machine with a similar name in another resource group is not a match: show the rehearsal capture instead.
steps.speaker: Say: and this is Azure's side: the same machine, now an Azure resource with its own identity and tags. Notice it has no Owner tag; we come back to that in the Policy demo.
steps.attendee: The Arc resource and the agent must agree on the same resource ID; that is what 'connected' means.

steps.title: What connecting did, and did not, do
steps.body: In the portal open Azure Arc > Machines > cas26-arcwin01 and show the Extensions page. Run the command to list the Arc machines in the operations resource group. Name what later demos add to this same resource: the Azure Monitor agent with its data collection rule (DCR) association, Defender for Cloud coverage, the Owner-tag policy and the Sentinel training event. Transition: the software that already runs these VMs, SCVMM and vCenter.
steps.code: az resource list --resource-group $Demo.OperationsResourceGroup --resource-type Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines --query '[].{name:name,id:id}' -o table
steps.expected: cas26-arcwin01 is in the list with the other on-premises Arc machines; the audience can see that Connected means manageable, not yet monitored, secured or proven to work.
steps.troubleshooting: If the list is slow or empty, stay on the portal page from step 5 and make the same point; nothing later depends on this command.
steps.speaker: Ask: which resource can we now govern? Then debrief: connecting creates the Azure representation; it does not turn on monitoring, Defender or Policy, and it says nothing yet about whether the application works. Transition: we connected these machines from the inside; next, the software that already runs these VMs, SCVMM and vCenter.
steps.attendee: Connecting makes a server manageable through Azure. Monitoring, security coverage, compliance and application health each need their own setup and their own evidence.

demos.title: Add AWS resources through the Arc multicloud connector
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: the Arc multicloud connector is one Azure resource that is given access to an AWS account, brings its resources into Azure and can onboard its EC2 servers and EKS clusters to Arc. We walk the four steps from the previous slides on a real connector: give Azure access, the connector, it brings things in, you manage them. The point is to tell three results apart: an AWS resource Azure only lists (inventory), an EC2 server that became an Arc-enabled server, and an EKS cluster that became an Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: pcc-tplabs-cas26-aws-eus-01 is the presenter's existing multicloud connector; AWS_<AccountId> is the resource group the connector creates for AWS resources (the portal may show it in lower case, aws_<accountId>); eks-iic-cas26-use2-01 is the EKS cluster; the eight EC2 machines are the six application servers of IIC Hybrid Orders (the sample application used throughout the session) plus two SQL Server machines; Event:cas26 is the AWS tag the connector filters on.

To reproduce: an AWS account where you can deploy the connector's CloudFormation template, an Azure subscription with the Microsoft.HybridConnectivity and Microsoft.HybridCompute resource providers registered, Contributor on the target resource group, and Azure CLI with the resource-graph, connectedmachine and connectedk8s extensions.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: the connector already exists; this demo inspects it and never creates one. Before delivery, review the AWS CloudFormation stack, account, regions, tag filters, connector identity and the enabled solutions.

Presenter lab: the landing-zone baseline (access, Defender, Sentinel, Policy) must cover the connector-created AWS_<AccountId> resource group; an operations-resource-group policy does not reach it. Check its effective baseline before allowing onboarding.

Presenter lab: discovery and onboarding run on the connector's own schedule. Do not create a duplicate Arc connection; the demo shows the configured solutions, the last sync time and the verified results.
demos.reset: Leave connector, source authorization and Arc resources intact for both sessions. No live reset; repeated onboarding is not the reset mechanism.
demos.fallback: If the portal or Resource Graph is slow, show the rehearsal capture of the connector, its solutions and the source-to-Azure identity pairs, and name the step you would have run.
demos.wait: Discovery and onboarding run asynchronously on the connector's schedule. Show the last synchronization time rather than waiting for a new scan.

steps.title: Find the connector and the AWS account behind it
steps.body: Load context (first line), then list the multicloud connectors in the subscription. In a browser tab next to the terminal, show the AWS console for the same account and region (no credentials on screen) and point at one EC2 instance ID and the EKS cluster ARN; step 5 follows those two into Azure.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
az resource list --resource-type Microsoft.HybridConnectivity/publicCloudConnectors --query '[].{name:name,id:id,resourceGroup:resourceGroup}' -o table
steps.expected: One connector, pcc-tplabs-cas26-aws-eus-01, with its resource group. The AWS tab shows the same account; the workloads stay in AWS.
steps.troubleshooting: If no connector is listed, check the signed-in subscription (az account show) first; the connector lives in the workload subscription. If several are listed, use the one above and say the others are out of scope.
steps.speaker: Say: the first step on the slide was give Azure access; the second is the connector itself. This is it: one Azure resource pointing at one AWS account. Nothing moved out of AWS.
steps.attendee: The connector is an Azure resource tied to one AWS account; the AWS workloads do not move.

steps.title: See which solutions the connector offers
steps.body: Run the lab helper below. It lists the solution types the connector service currently publishes for this subscription (inventory, Arc server onboarding, EKS onboarding and others) and the settings each accepts. We only read the list; nothing is changed.
steps.code: pwsh ./shared/foundation/scripts/Get-Cas26ConnectorSolutionTypes.ps1
steps.expected: A list of the available solution types and their settings, including inventory and the Arc onboarding solutions.
steps.troubleshooting: If it fails with a provider-registration or permission error, say so and show the rehearsal capture of the list. Do not register providers or change settings on stage.
steps.speaker: Say: the connector does nothing on its own; you choose solutions. Inventory only lists what exists. The onboarding solutions put the Arc agent on a server, or the Arc agents on a cluster.
steps.attendee: A connector's solutions are separate choices: inventory lists resources; onboarding solutions make them Arc-enabled.

steps.title: Walk the access grant and the chosen solutions
steps.body: In the Azure portal, open Azure Arc > Multicloud connectors > pcc-tplabs-cas26-aws-eus-01. Show the AWS account and regions, the Event:cas26 tag filter, and each solution (Inventory, Arc server onboarding, EKS onboarding, monitoring) with its last sync time. Then, in the AWS console, open the CloudFormation stack the connector asked us to deploy and show the IAM role it created: that role is how Azure was given access. Do not add or change anything.
steps.expected: The access grant (CloudFormation stack and its role), the tag filter and each solution's state and last sync time are visible; no new permission is granted.
steps.troubleshooting: If the stack shows an error or a solution is unhealthy, name it as a setup problem and show the rehearsal capture. Never widen the AWS role or remove the tag filter to make more resources appear.
steps.speaker: Say: this is 'give Azure access': a CloudFormation stack in AWS creates a role Azure may use, and nothing broader. The tag filter means only resources tagged Event:cas26 come in.
steps.attendee: Access is granted on the AWS side by a CloudFormation-created role; tag filters limit what the connector brings in.

steps.title: Where the AWS resources land in Azure
steps.body: Run the command to show the connector-created resource group and its tags. In the portal, open that resource group's Access control (IAM) and Policies pages and show that the same landing-zone rules apply here as to the on-premises machines.
steps.code: az group show --name $Demo.AwsResourceGroup --query '{id:id,name:name,tags:tags}' -o json
steps.expected: The AWS_<AccountId> resource group with its tags; its role assignments and policy assignments are visible in the portal.
steps.troubleshooting: A name that differs only in case (aws_<accountId>) is the same group. If the group is not found, compare AwsResourceGroup in demo.local.json with the portal.
steps.speaker: Say: 'it brings things in', and they land in their own resource group. That group needs the same access, security and Policy rules as everything else, or the AWS servers become the unmanaged corner of the estate.
steps.attendee: The connector creates its own resource group; make sure your landing-zone access and policy rules cover it.

steps.title: Tell the three results apart
steps.body: Run the four commands. The first uses Azure Resource Graph, because inventory records (the awsresources table) are not returned by an ordinary resource list. Then map each result: awsresources = Azure knows the AWS resource exists; Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines = an EC2 server that is now an Arc-enabled server; Microsoft.Kubernetes/connectedClusters = the EKS cluster, now an Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster. Match the EC2 instance ID and EKS ARN from step 1 to these resources.
steps.code:
az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.SubscriptionId -q "awsresources | where resourceGroup =~ '$($Demo.AwsResourceGroup)' | summarize count() by type" -o table
az resource list --resource-group $Demo.AwsResourceGroup --resource-type Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines --query '[].{name:name,status:properties.status,id:id}' -o table
az resource show --ids $Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId --query '{id:id,status:properties.status,agentVersion:properties.agentVersion,tags:tags}' -o json
az connectedk8s show --ids $Demo.EksArcResourceId --query '{id:id,connectivity:connectivityStatus,provisioning:provisioningState}' -o json
steps.expected: A count of AWS inventory by type; the eight EC2 Arc machines with status Connected; one EC2 Arc machine in detail (status Connected, agent version, tags); and the EKS cluster with connectivity Connected. Inventory presence alone does not prove an agent or cluster connection.
steps.troubleshooting: If a resource sits in an alternative resource group configured in demo.local.json, use that exact ID and say why. Never pair resources by display name alone. If Resource Graph is slow, show the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Say: three results, three different things. Inventory is only a list. An Arc-enabled server has the agent. An Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster has the Arc agents inside the cluster. EKS is still EKS; it has not become AKS.
steps.attendee: Inventory, an Arc-enabled server and an Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster are different states; inventory alone does not mean an agent is connected.

steps.title: Hand these resources to the rest of the session
steps.body: Read the result aloud: all eight CAS26 EC2 machines (six IIC application servers plus two SQL Server machines) are Arc Connected, and the EKS cluster eks-iic-cas26-use2-01 is Connected as an Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster. Say which ones come back: EC2 machines in the Observe, Secure and Policy demos, and the EKS cluster in the Flux demo. Transition: edge sites and legacy servers, where Arc still needs an outbound connection to Azure.
steps.expected: The audience knows which AWS resources the later demos use; no management result is claimed yet.
steps.troubleshooting: If a machine or the cluster shows Disconnected, say so and name the later demo it affects; never claim Connected from an inventory entry.
steps.speaker: Say: 'you manage them' is the rest of the session. A resource list is not management: later we change a Policy-managed tag on one of these EC2 servers and reconcile Kubernetes objects on this EKS cluster. Transition: edge sites and legacy servers.
steps.attendee: The connector gets AWS resources into Azure; monitoring, security, Policy and GitOps are the separate management steps that follow.

demos.title: Query the estate, then read machine and service health
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: two questions need two different places to ask. Azure Resource Graph answers 'what exists and how is it configured' right now; Log Analytics answers 'what happened over time', using data the Azure Monitor agent sends under a data collection rule (DCR). We then place one real order in the sample application and read machine health and service health side by side, because green servers do not prove that customers' orders complete.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: IIC Hybrid Orders is the session's sample application; each order passes through Azure, an on-premises worker and an AWS worker. Cas26Service_CL is the custom Log Analytics table where each order writes one row per stage. dcr-tplabs-cas26-linux-eus-01 is the data collection rule (DCR) for the Linux machines; dcr-cas26-requests-eus-01 is the DCR that receives the order records. hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01 is the Azure Monitor health model for the service. cas26-arcwin01 and cas26-lnx01 are the on-premises Arc machines.

To reproduce: Arc-enabled machines with the Azure Monitor agent and a DCR association to a Log Analytics workspace, Reader on the subscription and Log Analytics Reader on the workspace, and Azure CLI with the resource-graph, connectedmachine and log-analytics extensions. The order and health-model steps need an application of your own that writes one record per request.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: prepare browser tabs for Resource Graph Explorer, Log Analytics (Logs), the CAS26 service-operations workbook and the health model; check each tab's scope, workspace and time range beforehand.

The configured LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId is the workspace/customer GUID used by az monitor log-analytics query. It is distinct from the Sentinel workspace ARM resource ID and from an Azure Monitor workspace.

Presenter lab: machine evidence uses one of the EC2 Arc machines (Ec2ArcResourceId); the same queries work for the on-premises machines. ServiceUrl is the IIC order endpoint and HealthModelResourceId the health model. Place one rehearsal order and confirm its stage rows arrive in Cas26Service_CL.
demos.reset: Read-only. If a controlled fault is still active from the Whole-Service Observability session, its operator restores only that worker with Set-Cas26WorkerMode.ps1 -Mode Healthy, then places a new IIC order and checks fresh stage records. Do not fault or reset anything else.
demos.fallback: If a query or the portal is slow, show the rehearsal capture of the same query with its target, store, time window and collection timestamp, and name the step you would have run.
demos.wait: Ingestion and the query or view refresh are separate delays. The order result returned to the client is immediate, but its stage rows reach Log Analytics a few minutes later; say so and avoid repeated polling on stage.

steps.title: Ask Resource Graph what exists
steps.body: Load context, then run the Resource Graph query (the same query can be pasted into Resource Graph Explorer in the portal). It lists Arc machines, Azure VMs and Arc-enabled Kubernetes clusters in the operations and AWS resource groups of the selected subscription.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
$query = "Resources | where resourceGroup in~ ('$($Demo.OperationsResourceGroup)', '$($Demo.AwsResourceGroup)') | where type in~ ('microsoft.hybridcompute/machines','microsoft.compute/virtualmachines','microsoft.kubernetes/connectedclusters') | project name,type,resourceGroup,id,tags"
az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.SubscriptionId -q $query -o table
steps.expected: The on-premises Arc machines (including cas26-arcwin01 and cas26-lnx01) in the operations resource group; the eight EC2 Arc machines and the EKS connected cluster in the AWS resource group; each with type, resource group, ID and tags. This is current configuration, not history.
steps.troubleshooting: If the table is empty, confirm the subscription (az account show) and that OperationsResourceGroup and AwsResourceGroup in demo.local.json match the portal. Do not remove the resource-group filter just to get rows.
steps.speaker: Say: the first place to ask is Resource Graph: what exists right now and how it is configured, across Azure, our datacenter and AWS. It cannot tell us whether anything worked five minutes ago.
steps.attendee: Resource Graph answers inventory and configuration questions across every estate; it holds no history of performance or requests.

steps.title: Check the machine is set up to send data
steps.body: Run the two commands for the selected EC2 Arc machine: its resource, then its extensions. In the portal, open the same machine > Extensions and show AzureMonitorLinuxAgent; then open Monitor > Data Collection Rules > dcr-tplabs-cas26-linux-eus-01 > Resources and show this machine in the rule's DCR associations.
steps.code:
az resource show --ids $Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId --query '{id:id,identity:identity,tags:tags,properties:properties}' -o json
az connectedmachine extension list --machine-name ($Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId.Split('/')[-1]) --resource-group $Demo.AwsResourceGroup --query '[].{name:name,state:properties.provisioningState}' -o table
steps.expected: The extension list includes AzureMonitorLinuxAgent in state Succeeded, and the machine is listed under dcr-tplabs-cas26-linux-eus-01's resources.
steps.troubleshooting: If the agent or the DCR association is missing, say so: that is the first thing to check when a chart is empty. Do not show another machine's evidence instead.
steps.speaker: Say: slide 23 in practice. The agent is installed, the data collection rule says what to collect and where to send it, and the DCR association assigns that rule to this server. That is set-up, not proof that data is arriving.
steps.attendee: Agent plus DCR association is the set-up; only fresh data in the workspace proves collection works.

steps.title: Ask Log Analytics when the machine last reported
steps.body: Run the two KQL queries through the CLI (or paste them into Logs in the workspace). The first reads the newest Heartbeat row for this exact machine; the second counts CPU samples from the last 30 minutes. Compare LastSeen with the current UTC time.
steps.code:
$q = "Heartbeat | where TimeGenerated > ago(30m) | where _ResourceId =~ '$($Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId)' | summarize LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated) by Computer, _ResourceId"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
$q = "Perf | where TimeGenerated > ago(30m) | where _ResourceId =~ '$($Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId)' | where ObjectName == 'Processor' and CounterName == '% Processor Time' | summarize Samples=count(), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), AvgCpu=avg(CounterValue)"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $Demo.LogAnalyticsWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: A Heartbeat LastSeen within the last few minutes, and a non-zero Samples count with a recent LastSeen for Perf. No rows means missing, stale or uncollected evidence, not a healthy machine.
steps.troubleshooting: Check, in order: the workspace GUID, the DCR association, agent health, table permissions and the time window. Never widen the query to the whole estate and call someone else's heartbeat proof.
steps.speaker: Say: the second place to ask is Log Analytics: what happened over time. This machine sent a heartbeat moments ago and CPU samples in the last half hour. That is machine health, and it is still not what the customer sees.
steps.attendee: Heartbeat and performance data prove the machine is reporting; an empty result is missing evidence, not good news.

steps.title: Place one real order
steps.body: Run the order client. It places one demo-tagged order in IIC Hybrid Orders and prints its CorrelationId (the ID that follows the order through every stage), which copy of the portal served it (Origin: Azure or AWS), its overall status and the result of every stage. The first line stops the step if ServiceUrl is still a placeholder.
steps.code:
if ($Demo.ServiceUrl -match '^PENDING|REPLACE_WITH') { throw 'Populate ServiceUrl in demo.local.json with the IIC order endpoint before delivery.' }
$order = & ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 -BaseUri $Demo.ServiceUrl -DemoTag
$order | Select-Object CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Origin, Status, ElapsedMs
$order.Stages | Format-Table Cloud, Component, Stage, Success, DurationMs
steps.expected: Status Completed with a CorrelationId and an Origin, and a stage table in which every stage in Azure, on-premises and AWS shows Success True with its duration. A portal that loads is not an order that completed.
steps.troubleshooting: A failed stage can be a configured demo fault; check FailureMode before calling it an incident. A timeout may indicate a stuck queue or a missing worker. Preserve the actual response; do not manufacture a successful order.
steps.speaker: Say: slide 24, green servers, broken service. The only thing that proves the service works is a real order finishing. This one went through Azure, our datacenter and AWS.
steps.attendee: A completed request is the proof of service health; a portal that loads is not.

steps.title: Read order outcomes in the logs
steps.body: Run the queries. The first summarizes all IIC orders from the last 30 minutes: each order writes one row per stage, so rows are grouped by CorrelationId before counting orders, failed orders and unresolved orders. The second shows only the order from step 4, stage by stage, across the three clouds. Zero orders in the window means not enough evidence, not 0% failure.
steps.expected: Orders, FailedOrders, Unresolved, LastSeen and FailurePercent for the window; then the step 4 order's stage rows, once ingested (usually within a few minutes).
steps.troubleshooting: If the new order's rows have not arrived yet, say so and use the client output from step 4; ingestion delay is not a failure. sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/src/queries/service-overview.kql is the same order summary, ready to paste into the Logs blade.
steps.speaker: Say: the same order, now as evidence in the logs, one row per stage in each cloud. If it is not here yet, that is ingestion delay; the client output from step 4 already proved the order.
steps.attendee: Summarize per request before you count; stage-level rows otherwise overstate the number of orders.

steps.title: Read machine health and service health together
steps.body: Open the CAS26 service-operations workbook, then the health model hm-tplabs-cas26-service-cus-01 in the portal. For each workbook panel, name where its data comes from: Resource Graph (configuration), Log Analytics KQL (logs), platform metrics, or Azure Monitor workspace PromQL. In the health model, follow the rollup from slide 25: the customer order depends on Azure coordination, on-premises validation and AWS fulfillment; read each part's state and how fresh its evidence is, then who owns the next action and what would prove recovery. Run the command only to confirm you are on the right health model resource; health itself is read in the portal view. Mention once that the Whole-Service Observability session builds this model in depth. Transition to section 2, Secure.
steps.code:
if ($Demo.HealthModelResourceId -match '^PENDING|REPLACE_WITH') { throw 'Populate HealthModelResourceId in demo.local.json before delivery.' }
az resource show --ids $Demo.HealthModelResourceId --query '{id:id,location:location,provisioning:properties.provisioningState}' -o json
steps.expected: The audience can distinguish current metadata, machine condition and customer outcome. provisioning=Succeeded is deployment status, not health; health state is read in the Health Model view, and Unknown/stale evidence is explained according to the configured model, without a deep model-authoring detour.
steps.troubleshooting: If the command fails, check HealthModelResourceId in demo.local.json. If the view shows Unknown, explain it as missing or stale evidence under the model's rules, not as healthy. If the view will not load, show the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Say: three green lights answer three different questions: the server exists, the server is reporting, the order completed. Only the last one is what the customer feels. Ask: who acts next, and what would a new successful order prove? Transition: section 2, Secure: who is allowed to take that action, and how is it protected?
steps.attendee: Health views combine evidence under a chosen design. A green resource inventory row, a fresh heartbeat and a completed customer order answer different questions.

demos.title: Prove access to an Arc resource with Azure RBAC
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: being able to see a server in Azure and being allowed to change it are different permissions. Two real accounts try the same small, reversible change (adding a tag) on the same Arc-enabled server: the read-only account is refused, the operator account succeeds, and the Azure Activity Log records who did what. This is the Azure door from the four-doors slide and the people rule from the three-rules slide: read-only by default, change rights only through an approved, scoped role.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: iic-cas26-prd-web-01 is an AWS EC2 server of the sample application, Arc-enabled through the connector (Ec2RbacArcResourceId); cas26-test-* are cloud-only test users and sg-tplabs-cas26-* the security groups that hold their roles; CAS26RbacProof is a tag reserved for this demo.

To reproduce: one Arc-enabled server, two accounts (one with Reader, one with a narrow role that can write tags, such as Tag Contributor, at the resource group or on the machine), and two terminals signed in separately (give each its own AZURE_CONFIG_DIR).

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: check inherited assignments, group memberships and active PIM roles for both accounts; a Reader assignment does not cancel a broader inherited role. Pre-stage the role assignments; never grant broad permissions during the demo.
Presenter lab: use two already-authenticated terminal and browser profiles with distinct AZURE_CONFIG_DIR values. Do not swap tokens or simulate roles.

Presenter lab: CAS26RbacProof goes on iic-cas26-prd-web-01 only, never on the Policy demo's target (iic-cas26-prd-api-01), so rehearsal tag writes cannot disturb that demo's before-state. It changes the Azure tag only, never the native AWS instance tag. Record whether the tag exists before the demo. The Owner-tag policy touches only the Owner tag, so CAS26RbacProof has no policy side effect.

Presenter lab: choose the reader and operator from the cas26-test-* users and the sg-tplabs-cas26-* groups, and verify their role assignments at the AWS_<AccountId> resource group or on the exact machine.
demos.reset: Restore only the reserved tag from the recorded baseline; preserve activity history. Remove temporary CAS26 role assignments only if separately created for preparation and after verifying no other session depends on them. Keep prepared identities for rehearsals.
demos.fallback: If sign-in or the portal is slow, show the rehearsal capture from the two real principals (the denial, the successful write and the Activity Log entries) and name the step you would have run. Never emulate a denial with fabricated output.
demos.wait: Role and PIM changes and Activity Log ingestion take time to appear; activate and check access beforehand. Never grant a broader role to get around a propagation delay.

steps.title: Show the two accounts
steps.body: In each of the two terminals (reader first, then operator), load context and show the signed-in account. In the portal, open the machine > Access control (IAM) > Check access and look up each account to show its effective roles, including anything inherited from the resource group or a group membership.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
az account show --query '{principal:user.name,type:user.type,tenant:tenantId,subscription:id}' -o json
steps.expected: Two different user names on the same tenant and subscription; Check access shows Reader for the reader and the scoped tag-writing role for the operator.
steps.troubleshooting: If both terminals show the same user, AZURE_CONFIG_DIR is not separate: stop and fix it before any write. If Check access shows a broader inherited role for the reader, the refusal in step 3 will not happen; say so and use the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Say: of the four doors into a server, this demo tests only the Azure door, whose key is an Azure role. And it shows the people rule live: read-only by default, change rights only through an approved, scoped role (in production, activated through PIM for a limited time after MFA).
steps.attendee: Check effective access, including inherited and group roles, not only the assignment you expect.

steps.title: The reader can see the server
steps.body: In the reader terminal, read the EC2 Arc machine and its tags. Note whether CAS26RbacProof is already present: that is the baseline to restore in step 6 (normally it is absent).
steps.code: az resource show --ids $Demo.Ec2RbacArcResourceId --query '{id:id,tags:tags,identity:identity}' -o json
steps.expected: The read succeeds and shows the machine ID, its tags (normally without CAS26RbacProof) and its managed identity.
steps.troubleshooting: If the read fails, the reader lacks Reader at this scope or the terminal is on the wrong subscription; check step 1 and show the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Say: the reader can see everything about this server in Azure. That key opens the Azure door only: it does not let anyone sign in to the server, stop the VM in AWS, or read the application's data.
steps.attendee: Reader access is visibility only; it does not open the sign-in, hosting or application doors.

steps.title: The reader tries a change and is refused
steps.body: Still in the reader terminal, run the tag update. This is a real write request that is expected to be refused; the script stops if the write unexpectedly succeeds. Read the error aloud: AuthorizationFailed, naming the account, the action (Microsoft.Resources/tags/write) and the scope.
steps.code:
az tag update --resource-id $Demo.Ec2RbacArcResourceId --operation Merge --tags CAS26RbacProof=operator-verified
$ReaderWriteExitCode = $LASTEXITCODE
if ($ReaderWriteExitCode -eq 0) { throw 'Unexpected write success: stop, inspect effective privileges, and restore the reserved tag.' }
# Inspect the actual error: AuthorizationFailed is expected; network/CLI errors do not prove RBAC denial.
steps.expected: An AuthorizationFailed error naming the reader account, the tags write action and the machine's scope; the script does not throw.
steps.troubleshooting: A network or CLI error is not a refusal and proves nothing about access: fix it and rerun, or show the capture. If the update succeeds, the reader has more rights than intended: stop, find the inherited, group or PIM role, keep the honest result, and restore the tag as in step 6.
steps.speaker: Say: same server, same command, and Azure says no, and says exactly why: this account, this action, this scope.
steps.attendee: A real refused request, with its error, proves a permission boundary; a hidden button in the portal does not.

steps.title: The operator makes the same change
steps.body: In the operator terminal, run exactly the same tag update; the second command reads the tags back. No role is created or widened on stage.
steps.expected: The update succeeds and the tags now include CAS26RbacProof=operator-verified; every other tag is unchanged.
steps.troubleshooting: If a deny assignment or policy blocks the action, explain the additional boundary. Do not disable it to make the demonstration work.
steps.speaker: Say: the only difference is the account and its role. The operator holds a narrow role that can write tags, at this scope only.
steps.attendee: Change rights come from a scoped role on the right account, not from being an administrator everywhere.

steps.title: Who did what: the Activity Log
steps.body: Run the Activity Log query for the last hour (or open the machine > Activity log in the portal). Find the tag write and read its time, caller, operation, status and correlation ID.
steps.code: az monitor activity-log list --resource-id $Demo.Ec2RbacArcResourceId --offset 1h --query '[].{time:eventTimestamp,caller:caller,operation:operationName.value,status:status.value,correlation:correlationId}' -o table
steps.expected: A successful tag write whose caller is the operator account, at the time of step 4. The refused attempt may also appear as a failed write; if it has not arrived yet, the CLI error from step 3 is the evidence.
steps.troubleshooting: Activity Log can lag; do not infer caller from the currently open portal session. Read the recorded caller and correlation ID.
steps.speaker: Say: every control-plane change is recorded with who made it. That record is what an auditor asks for.
steps.attendee: The Azure Activity Log records who changed what and when; it is the evidence of an authorized change.

steps.title: Put the tag back and close
steps.body: In the operator terminal, restore the baseline recorded in step 2. Normally CAS26RbacProof was absent, so run the commands below: they remove only that key and read the tags again. If it had an earlier value, set that value back in the portal (machine > Tags) instead. Close on the trap from the four-doors slide.
steps.code:
# Normal case: CAS26RbacProof did not exist before the demo, so remove only that key.
az tag update --resource-id $Demo.Ec2RbacArcResourceId --operation Delete --tags CAS26RbacProof=operator-verified
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Tag restore failed: remove CAS26RbacProof in the portal (machine > Tags) before moving on.' }
az resource show --ids $Demo.Ec2RbacArcResourceId --query tags -o json
steps.expected: CAS26RbacProof is gone (or back to its recorded value), every other tag is unchanged, and no temporary broad role exists. Management permission is distinguished from signing in to the server.
steps.troubleshooting: If the delete fails, remove CAS26RbacProof in the portal (machine > Tags) as the operator before moving on; never leave the reserved tag behind for the next session.
steps.speaker: Close on the trap: an Azure role that can run commands or install extensions is admin access inside the server, so hand it out like server admin. Debrief: account, role, scope, allowed action, refused action and the Activity Log record. That was the people rule; the fix-up tools rule returns in the Policy demo, whose remediation identity can change tags in one resource group only. Transition: knowing who can act does not tell us what is weak or under attack; that is Defender for Cloud.
steps.attendee: RBAC evaluates effective access from all applicable assignments. Four doors, four keys: an Azure role opens the Azure door only, and reader visibility, management rights and guest sign-in are related but distinct security decisions.

demos.title: Inspect a Defender for Cloud finding for an Arc-enabled server
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: Defender for Cloud only shows findings for a server when its Defender for Servers plan is on and the Defender for Endpoint sensor runs on that server. We follow that chain on one Arc-enabled AWS server: check the coverage, open one real finding about what is weak (a security recommendation), and turn it into an action with an owner and a way to prove it was fixed. A finding nobody owns is just a red badge.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: the target is iic-cas26-prd-api-01, one of the sample application's Linux EC2 servers, Arc-enabled through the connector (Ec2ArcResourceId); AWS_<AccountId> is the connector-created resource group.

To reproduce: Defender for Servers enabled on the subscription, an Arc-enabled server with the Defender for Endpoint sensor, Security Reader (or higher) in Defender for Cloud, and Azure CLI with the resource-graph extension.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: Defender for Servers Plan 2 is enabled on the workload, management and security subscriptions. Confirm coverage for the AWS and on-premises Arc machines before either session; Arc registration by itself is not Defender coverage.

Presenter lab: preselect one current Linux security-baseline recommendation on the target machine (each IIC Linux machine carries about 40 hardening findings). Never introduce a vulnerability into the shared environment to create one.

Presenter lab: record the finding's resource ID, assessment time, evidence, remediation owner, change window and how the fix will be verified. Keep unrelated security findings off the projected screen.
demos.reset: Read-only by default. Preserve real security records and audit history. Do not dismiss findings, weaken controls or reboot shared workloads as a reset.
demos.fallback: If Defender for Cloud is slow to load, show the rehearsal capture of the finding with its resource ID, assessment time and owner, and name the step you would have run. Never invent a finding to fill an empty screen.
demos.wait: Assessments refresh on the service's schedule. Read the assessment time rather than waiting for a refresh, and never promise immediate clearance after a change.

steps.title: Pick the exact server
steps.body: Load context and show the selected EC2 Arc machine. Then open Microsoft Defender for Cloud > Inventory in the portal and filter to the AWS_<AccountId> resource group and this machine's name.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
az resource show --ids $Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId --query '{id:id,name:name,tags:tags}' -o json
steps.expected: The machine's ID, name and tags in the terminal, and the same machine in Defender for Cloud's inventory; similarly named resources are excluded.
steps.troubleshooting: If the machine is missing from the inventory, check the portal's directory and subscription filter. A similarly named machine elsewhere is not a substitute: show the rehearsal capture.
steps.speaker: Say: the same AWS server we have been following. First make sure the portal and the terminal look at the same machine.
steps.attendee: Start a security investigation by pinning down the exact resource ID.

steps.title: Check the chain: plan and sensor
steps.body: In Defender for Cloud > Environment settings, open the subscription and show Defender for Servers is On (Plan 2). Then, on the machine's page in Inventory, show that the Defender for Endpoint sensor (the MDE.Linux extension) is installed and healthy, and read when the machine was last assessed. Not every plan uses the Log Analytics workspace; say which component supplies this evidence.
steps.expected: Defender for Servers Plan 2 On for the subscription; the machine shows the Defender for Endpoint sensor installed and a recent assessment time. A missing sensor or a stale assessment is visible, not hidden.
steps.troubleshooting: If coverage shows a gap, name it as a configuration finding: without the plan and the sensor there are no vulnerability findings or security alerts from this path. Never enable a billable plan on stage to fill the page.
steps.speaker: Say: this is the chain from the last slide. You turn on the Defender for Servers plan; the plan puts the Defender for Endpoint sensor on the server; what the sensor finds comes back here. No plan, no sensor, no findings.
steps.attendee: Check plan and sensor coverage before trusting an empty findings list.

steps.title: Open one finding: what is weak
steps.body: From the machine, open Recommendations and choose the preselected Linux security-baseline recommendation. Read the affected resource, severity, status, the last assessment time and which setting is wrong. Follow attack-path context only if the page actually shows it.
steps.expected: One recommendation tied to this exact machine, with severity, status Unhealthy, an assessment time and the failing configuration: an attributable target and evidence, not merely a severity badge.
steps.troubleshooting: If the chosen recommendation no longer applies, show that as a legitimate change. Do not substitute an unrelated finding or imply unavailable attack-path features are enabled.
steps.speaker: Say: this is posture, what is weak. A security alert would be protection, what is under attack. They are different results and they go to different people.
steps.attendee: Recommendations say what is weak; security alerts say what is under attack. Know which one you are looking at.

steps.title: Decide who fixes it
steps.body: Open the recommendation's remediation steps. Say who owns the fix, what access they need, when it can be done, what it could affect and how you will check it worked. Show the owner in the team's existing workflow (for example the recommendation's owner assignment or a ticket) rather than inventing one on stage.
steps.expected: A named owner (person or team), a change window and a verification step for this one finding; a resource Owner tag alone does not prove anyone accepted the work.
steps.troubleshooting: If a patch/reboot would disrupt the shared service, explain the planned action rather than performing it. The demo goal is evidence-to-decision, not an improvised production change.
steps.speaker: Say: the chain ends with an owner. A finding with no owner does not get fixed, and an Owner tag on the resource is not the same as someone accepting the work.
steps.attendee: Every finding needs an owner, a window and a way to verify the fix.

steps.title: Check how fresh the status is
steps.body: Run the Resource Graph query. It lists every Defender assessment for this machine with its status, severity, when it was first evaluated and when its status last changed. If a fix was applied during preparation, show the before and after with their times; otherwise name the planned change and its window.
steps.code:
$q = "securityresources | where type == 'microsoft.security/assessments' | where tostring(properties.resourceDetails.Id) =~ '$($Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId)' | project Recommendation=tostring(properties.displayName), Status=tostring(properties.status.code), Severity=tostring(properties.metadata.severity), FirstEvaluated=todatetime(properties.status.firstEvaluationDate), StatusChanged=todatetime(properties.status.statusChangeDate) | order by Status asc, Severity asc"
az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.SubscriptionId -q $q --first 100 -o table
steps.expected: A table of this machine's assessments with Healthy or Unhealthy status and their dates; the chosen finding is present with its status-change date. Assessment refresh delay is acknowledged.
steps.troubleshooting: A successful patch command is not automatically a refreshed Defender assessment. Do not mark the finding resolved based solely on command completion.
steps.speaker: Say: a status is only as good as its timestamp. A fix is proven when a fresh assessment says Healthy, not when the patch command finishes.
steps.attendee: A finding is fixed when a fresh assessment says so, not when the change command completes.

steps.title: Debrief and hand over to Sentinel
steps.body: Summarize: coverage checked, one finding on the exact server, an owner, and fresh evidence to prove the fix. Recall who is allowed to act from the RBAC demo. Transition: Defender for Cloud shows what is weak or under attack on each resource; Microsoft Sentinel brings security data from servers and cloud services into one workspace and turns it into incidents.
steps.expected: The audience can tell a Defender recommendation from a security alert and from a Sentinel incident.
steps.troubleshooting: Nothing to run here. If an earlier step fell back to a capture, name what it would have shown before moving on.
steps.speaker: Say: one finding, deep enough to act on; we are not touring every Defender page. Transition: Microsoft Sentinel, where security data from many sources becomes one investigation.
steps.attendee: Security findings become useful when target, freshness, owner and verification are clear. Service coverage and data integrations determine what evidence is available.

demos.title: Investigate a Microsoft Sentinel incident
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: Microsoft Sentinel collects security data into a Log Analytics workspace, runs detection rules over it and raises incidents for an analyst to own. We follow one harmless, clearly labelled training event from a Windows server (collected by the Azure Monitor agent under a data collection rule) through a detection rule into an incident, then record an owner and a decision. Nothing here is a real attack.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: cas26-arcwin01 is the on-premises Windows server connected in the first demo; law-tplabs-cas26-security-eus-01 is the Log Analytics workspace with Sentinel enabled; CAS26Demo is the event source and 2601 the event ID of the training event; incidents from the training rule are titled CAS26 TRAINING.

To reproduce: a Sentinel-enabled workspace; a Windows Arc-enabled server with the Azure Monitor agent and a data collection rule (DCR) that sends Application-log events to that workspace; a scheduled analytics rule on the training marker (src/queries/sentinel-training-event.kql); and Microsoft Sentinel Responder to assign and close incidents.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: Sentinel is onboarded on law-tplabs-cas26-security-eus-01 with the CAS26 training analytics rule. cas26-arcwin01 has AMA and a DCR association that routes Application-log events into that workspace. Confirm the rule and its incident settings; both sessions use the same shared baseline.

Presenter lab: run the training event before the live slot and confirm that the event and the incident actually exist. Read scripts/Write-Cas26Event.ps1 before choosing where to run it (it needs Windows).
Limit the view to CAS26 TRAINING incidents. Do not simulate malicious behavior, change production detection rules or close unrelated incidents.
demos.reset: Close/comment only the identified training incident according to the exercise contract. Keep rule and collection configuration for the next session. Do not delete incident history or disable a shared rule.
demos.fallback: If ingestion or the incident queue is slow, show the rehearsal capture of event, rule and incident with workspace and timestamps, and name the step you would have run.
demos.wait: Event ingestion plus the scheduled rule can take several minutes. Generate and verify the training event before the session and open the incident it created, rather than waiting for a new incident live.

steps.title: Confirm the Sentinel workspace
steps.body: Load context and show the Sentinel workspace resource. In the Defender portal (or Microsoft Sentinel in the Azure portal), open the same workspace and set the time range to the last 24 hours. The full resource ID proves which workspace; its GUID (customer ID) is what the query commands in steps 3 and 4 use.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
az resource show --ids $Demo.SentinelWorkspaceResourceId --query '{id:id,name:name,location:location}' -o json
steps.expected: The workspace name law-tplabs-cas26-security-eus-01 and its location, and the portal on the same workspace; not a similarly named one.
steps.troubleshooting: If the read fails, check SentinelWorkspaceResourceId in demo.local.json; the workspace sits in the security subscription, so the signed-in account needs read access there too.
steps.speaker: Say: the Sentinel slide said everything lands in one workspace. This is that workspace.
steps.attendee: Confirm the workspace before reading incidents; a similarly named workspace can hold different data.

steps.title: The harmless training event and the rule
steps.body: Before the session, on cas26-arcwin01, in PowerShell 7 at the repository root, run the command below. It writes one Information event (source CAS26Demo, ID 2601) to the Windows Application log. If CAS26Demo is not registered yet, run the script once with -RegisterSource in an elevated session first. Never run it on the presenter laptop. On stage, open Sentinel > Analytics and show the training rule: its query, schedule and incident settings.
steps.code:
# On the selected Windows guest, from its repository root:
pwsh ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Write-Cas26Event.ps1 -Message 'CAS26 Sentinel training'
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'Training event creation failed.' }
# The source must already have been registered during preparation.
steps.expected: Before the session: the script exits cleanly on the guest. On stage: the rule's query matches the CAS26Demo marker, with its frequency and incident creation turned on. It matches a known synthetic marker; it does not claim to detect a real attack.
steps.troubleshooting: If the script says the source is not registered, run it once with -RegisterSource in an elevated session on the guest and rerun. If the rule is disabled or missing, show the rehearsal capture; never edit a shared rule on stage.
steps.speaker: Say: this event is a harmless marker we wrote on purpose so the rule has something to find. It is not an attack, and the rule does not claim to detect one.
steps.attendee: Use a clearly labelled synthetic event to test a detection path end to end.

steps.title: Check the event reached Sentinel
steps.body: Back in the presenter terminal, run the commands. They look up the Sentinel workspace's own GUID (the monitoring workspace from the Observe demo is a different workspace) and query its Event table for the training marker from the last hour. Match the computer, the marker text and a recent timestamp before opening any incident.
steps.code:
$SentinelWorkspaceId = az resource show --ids $Demo.SentinelWorkspaceResourceId --query properties.customerId -o tsv
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0 -or -not $SentinelWorkspaceId) { throw 'Cannot resolve the Sentinel workspace customer GUID.' }
$q = "Event | where TimeGenerated > ago(1h) | where Source == 'CAS26Demo' and EventID == 2601 | where RenderedDescription has 'CAS26 Sentinel training' | project TimeGenerated,Computer,RenderedDescription"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $SentinelWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: At least one row from cas26-arcwin01 with the text CAS26 Sentinel training and a recent TimeGenerated.
steps.troubleshooting: If no event appears, check in this order: the event on the guest (Event Viewer > Application), the Application-log DCR and its DCR association, the workspace the DCR sends to, and ingestion delay. SecurityEvent is a different table; do not switch tables to get rows.
steps.speaker: Say: the Sentinel slide in practice. The server's events come in through the same agent and data collection rule we saw in Observe. Data first; then the rule runs over it.
steps.attendee: A scheduled detection depends on the right data reaching the right workspace; the analytics rule cannot compensate for missing collection.

steps.title: Find the incident
steps.body: Run the query; it lists the latest state of each CAS26 TRAINING incident from the last 24 hours. Then open Incidents in the portal, filter on CAS26 TRAINING and open the newest one. The portal queue is where you work; the query is corroboration.
steps.code:
$SentinelWorkspaceId = az resource show --ids $Demo.SentinelWorkspaceResourceId --query properties.customerId -o tsv
if (-not $SentinelWorkspaceId) { throw 'Could not resolve the Sentinel workspace customer GUID.' }
$q = "SecurityIncident | where TimeGenerated > ago(24h) | summarize arg_max(TimeGenerated, *) by IncidentName | where Title startswith 'CAS26 TRAINING' | project IncidentNumber,Title,Severity,Status,Owner,CreatedTime"
az monitor log-analytics query --workspace $SentinelWorkspaceId --analytics-query $q -o table
steps.expected: One or more CAS26 TRAINING incidents with number, severity, status and created time, and the same incident in the portal queue, linked to the training rule.
steps.troubleshooting: If SecurityIncident is unavailable, inspect the configured Sentinel incident queue. No incident may mean ingestion, rule scheduling, suppression/grouping or incident creation settings need checking; do not create a false screenshot.
steps.speaker: Say: the rule found the marker and raised an incident. An incident is a case for a person to own, not an alarm to silence.
steps.attendee: A detection turns data into an incident; the incident queue is where an analyst takes ownership.

steps.title: Follow the evidence and entities
steps.body: In the incident, open the timeline, the alert and the underlying event. Match the computer (cas26-arcwin01), source and event ID, message and timestamps. Open the investigation graph only if the rule maps entities; missing entities are a rule-design gap, not an invisible successful investigation.
steps.expected: The incident is connected to the actual harmless event from cas26-arcwin01, with matching times.
steps.troubleshooting: Confirm table/connector permissions and time zones. An incident title alone does not prove the end-to-end data path.
steps.speaker: Say: read what was actually observed: this server, this event, this time. Anything beyond that is the analyst's hypothesis.
steps.attendee: The incident is connected to an actual harmless event from the selected guest.

steps.title: Record the owner and the decision
steps.body: Assign the prepared training owner (if this account may) and add a short comment: the signal is a benign CAS26 exercise, and here is what was verified. Do not run playbooks or containment against real hosts.
steps.expected: Only the training incident is updated; ownership and a reasoned response are preserved in its history.
steps.troubleshooting: If incident-write access is intentionally unavailable, show existing ownership and state the intended action. Do not elevate access during the talk.
steps.speaker: Say: every incident needs an owner and a written decision, even a training one.
steps.attendee: Record who owns an incident and why it was decided in the incident itself, so its history explains the outcome.

steps.title: Close the exercise without hiding history
steps.body: If the exercise calls for closure, close only this training incident with a benign/training classification and a comment. Show the recorded status. Transition to section 3, Govern: which team owns it, and does it stay the way we agreed?
steps.expected: The training record retains its investigation/decision history; no claim of containing a real attack is made.
steps.troubleshooting: If this account may not close incidents, leave it assigned with its comment and say so; never raise permissions on stage.
steps.speaker: Bridge: the data path and the response depended on things set up in advance: the workspace, the roles, collection and the rule. Keeping that set-up consistent across every estate is governance. Transition: section 3, Govern.
steps.attendee: Sentinel incident handling depends on configured data sources, analytics and entity mapping. An incident is evidence requiring interpretation; it is not proof that a threat has been contained.

demos.title: Evaluate and remediate Arc machines with Azure Policy — on-premises, then AWS
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: this runs the Require-an-Owner-tag policy from the two Azure Policy slides (39 and 40) on two real Arc-enabled servers: first the on-premises server connected in the first demo, then an AWS EC2 server onboarded by the connector. For each we walk the boxes of 'How Azure Policy works': definition and assignment, an evaluation that finds the Owner tag missing (NonCompliant), a remediation task in which the Modify effect adds the tag, and a fresh check that agrees. Same policy, same steps, two hosting locations.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: cas26-arcwin01 is the on-premises Windows server (pass 1); iic-cas26-prd-api-01 is an AWS EC2 server of the sample application (pass 2). tplabs-cas26-require-owner-tag-modify is the policy assignment on the operations resource group rg-tplabs-cas26-ops-eus-01; cas26-modify-owner-tag-aws-arc is the policy definition assigned separately on the connector-created AWS_<AccountId> resource group. Both add a missing Owner tag with the Modify effect.

To reproduce: a policy that adds a missing Owner tag with the Modify effect (the built-in 'Add a tag to resources' works), assigned at your resource group with a system-assigned managed identity that holds Tag Contributor there, and enforcement mode DoNotEnforce so the missing tag stays visible until you remediate (step 3 explains why). You need Resource Policy Contributor to create remediation tasks, and Azure CLI with the resource-graph extension.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab, pass 1: cas26-arcwin01 (OnPremArcResourceId) was connected in the first demo with Event=cas26 and no Owner tag, so the operations-resource-group assignment (PolicyAssignmentId) evaluates it NonCompliant. Record its tags before the demo.

Presenter lab, pass 2: iic-cas26-prd-api-01 (Ec2ArcResourceId) under the AWS-resource-group assignment of cas26-modify-owner-tag-aws-arc (Ec2PolicyAssignmentId). The operations assignment cannot reach the connector-created resource group, and its Event=cas26 filter never matches connector-created machines, so the second assignment is required; it allowlists the six IIC application machines by exact name, so every other machine in that group is outside its scope.

Presenter lab: verify both assignments and the definition: scope, enforcementMode=DoNotEnforce, parameters and defaults (tagValue may come from the definition default), exclusions, managed identity and its Tag Contributor role at the exact scope. DoNotEnforce is deliberate: in Default mode the Arc agents' routine status writes fire the Modify effect and tag every matching machine within seconds, leaving nothing to remediate. Do not switch either assignment to Default before the session.

Presenter lab: never remove a genuine owner tag to stage noncompliance. Between rehearsals reset by deleting the Owner tag on the Arc resource only (az tag update --operation Delete); rehearse on a dev EC2 machine and keep iic-cas26-prd-api-01 for delivery.
Presenter lab: a native AWS tag is separate from the Arc resource's Owner tag; pass 2 changes Azure metadata only. Do not use the RBAC demo's machine (Ec2RbacArcResourceId) in this demo.
demos.reset: Keep the corrected tags for the next session. Between rehearsals delete only the Owner tag on the demonstrated Arc representations; because both assignments are DoNotEnforce the tag stays absent until the next remediation task. Never disable Policy or remove a genuine owner. Retain task history; removing a task is not undoing its tag change. No native AWS tags, EC2 lifecycle or connector settings are changed.
demos.fallback: If a remediation task or evaluation is slow, read the tag directly from the resource, show the rehearsal capture of the completed task and fresh evaluation for that pass, and name the step you would have run. Never present a second AWS machine as the on-premises guest.
demos.wait: Remediation and the following Policy and Resource Graph refresh are separate asynchronous stages in each pass. Do not loop until green: read the resource, note the evaluation timestamp and move on.

steps.title: Pass 1: the on-premises server, before
steps.body: Load context and set the two variables for pass 1: the target is cas26-arcwin01 and the assignment is the operations resource group's Owner-tag assignment. Run the resource read and point at the tags: Event=cas26 is there, Owner is not. Nothing was removed to stage this; the server was connected without an Owner tag in the first demo.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
$TargetId = $Demo.OnPremArcResourceId
$AssignmentId = $Demo.PolicyAssignmentId
az resource show --ids $TargetId --query '{id:id,type:type,tags:tags,properties:properties}' -o json
steps.expected: The Microsoft.HybridCompute/machines resource for cas26-arcwin01, with tags that include Event=cas26 and no Owner tag.
steps.troubleshooting: If an Owner tag is already present, a rehearsal left it: say so, show the task history from that rehearsal instead of deleting the tag live, and go to pass 2. If the read fails, check OnPremArcResourceId in demo.local.json.
steps.speaker: Say: the same server we connected at the start; now we manage it. This is the running example from the Policy slides, the Require-an-Owner-tag policy, and this server has no Owner tag.
steps.attendee: Record a resource's tags before a governance change so you can prove what changed.

steps.title: Read the definition and the assignment
steps.body: Run the commands. The first prints the assignment: its scope (the operations resource group), enforcement mode (DoNotEnforce), parameters and managed identity. The second prints the definition it points to: the rule 'if the Owner tag is missing, Modify adds it', and the default tag value. Point out that the assignment sets no tag value, so the definition's default decides it. The policy adds a missing Owner tag; it does not repair an empty or wrong one.
steps.code:
$assignment = az rest --method get --url ($AssignmentId + '?api-version=2022-06-01') | ConvertFrom-Json
$assignment | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20
$definition = az rest --method get --url ($assignment.properties.policyDefinitionId + '?api-version=2023-04-01') | ConvertFrom-Json
$definition | ConvertTo-Json -Depth 20
steps.expected: Assignment scope = the operations resource group, enforcementMode = DoNotEnforce, a SystemAssigned identity; the definition has a Modify effect that adds the Owner tag and a default value that is a placeholder, not a real owner.
steps.troubleshooting: If the ID is an initiative, select its exact definition reference before proceeding. Do not run the standalone-policy command unchanged. If resolved value is a placeholder, describe placeholder compliance; do not claim it equals the configured ExpectedOwner.
steps.speaker: Say: the first two boxes on the 'How Azure Policy works' slide. The definition is the rule; the assignment says where it applies. And the default value it writes is a placeholder, not a person.
steps.attendee: Read the assignment and the definition together: default parameter values decide the outcome when the assignment is silent.

steps.title: Who may fix it, and why it is still NonCompliant
steps.body: In the portal, open Policy > Assignments > the assignment > Managed identity, and its role assignments: Tag Contributor on the operations resource group only. Then run the compliance query for this one server and this one assignment and read the state and timestamp. Explain why it is still NonCompliant: the assignment runs in DoNotEnforce, so the server's routine status updates did not trigger the Modify effect (in Default mode it would have been tagged within seconds, leaving nothing to show).
steps.code: az policy state list --resource $TargetId --filter "PolicyAssignmentId eq '$AssignmentId'" --query '[].{state:complianceState,time:timestamp,assignment:policyAssignmentId,definition:policyDefinitionId,resource:resourceId}' -o table
steps.expected: One row: complianceState NonCompliant, with a timestamp, this assignment and this server; the remediation identity can write tags at this scope.
steps.troubleshooting: No row is not compliance. Wait for evaluation in preparation. ExistingNonCompliant needs an evaluated noncompliant result; do not broaden the resource selection. If already compliant, inspect prior evidence rather than deleting a tag live.
steps.speaker: Say: the middle boxes: evaluate, then NonCompliant, and the reason is the missing Owner tag. The fix will run as the assignment's own identity, which can change tags in this one resource group and nothing else. That is the fix-up tools rule from the three rules.
steps.attendee: A current applicable NonCompliant row identifies a genuinely absent tag, and the remediation identity can perform the rule's operation.

steps.title: Run one remediation task: Modify adds the tag
steps.body: Create a remediation task for this one server under this one assignment; the name includes the time so it is unique. The task fixes only resources already evaluated as NonCompliant. No name filter, resource-group-wide remediation or re-evaluation discovery is used.
steps.expected: JSON for the new task with this assignment, this server and provisioningState Accepted or Evaluating. Accepted is not done.
steps.troubleshooting: If permission or evaluation fails, retain the error and use genuine before/after evidence. Do not assign broader permissions or change effect/definition during the demo.
steps.speaker: Say: the remediation task box. One task, one server, one assignment, running as the assignment's identity.
steps.attendee: The task targets the selected resource under the selected assignment; acceptance of the request is not completion.

steps.title: Check the task and read the tag
steps.body: Run the commands: the task's status, then the server's tags read straight from the resource. Compare the Owner value with the definition default from step 2 and with ExpectedOwner in demo.local.json.
steps.code:
az policy remediation show --resource $TargetId --name $RemediationName -o json
az resource show --ids $TargetId --query '{id:id,tags:tags}' -o json
steps.expected: The task shows Succeeded with the resource remediated; the tags now include Owner with the governed value, and every other tag is unchanged.
steps.troubleshooting: A task can have zero remediated resources or failures. Read counts/errors. Policy compliance may lag the direct resource read.
steps.speaker: Say: the tag is there. That proves the control works. It does not prove a person has accepted ownership; the placeholder value makes that gap visible.
steps.attendee: Task result and actual resource property agree; unrelated tags remain unchanged.

steps.title: Pass 1 result: a fresh check agrees
steps.body: Run the Resource Graph read and the compliance query again and compare the timestamp with step 3. If the new evaluation has not arrived yet, say 'evaluation pending' and rely on the tag readback from step 5. Then go straight to pass 2 in the same terminal.
steps.code:
az graph query --subscriptions $Demo.SubscriptionId -q "Resources | where id =~ '$TargetId' | project id,name,tags" -o json
az policy state list --resource $TargetId --filter "PolicyAssignmentId eq '$AssignmentId'" --query '[].{state:complianceState,time:timestamp,resource:resourceId}' -o table
steps.expected: Resource Graph shows the Owner tag; the compliance row shows Compliant with a newer timestamp, or still the old row while re-evaluation is pending. Do not announce Compliant until the timestamp supports it.
steps.troubleshooting: ARG and Policy are eventually consistent. Preserve direct read evidence and explicitly say reevaluation pending if that is the result.
steps.speaker: Say: the last box on the slide: after the fix, a fresh check agrees. Read the timestamp before you say Compliant.
steps.attendee: Changed Azure resource state and a fresh policy evaluation are distinct evidence. Do not announce fresh compliance until the timestamp supports it.

steps.title: Pass 2: switch to the AWS server
steps.body: Change only the two variables.
