The command block reads the EC2 Arc machine in the connector-created resource group and its compliance under the AWS-resource-group assignment: same definition, an allowlist of the six IIC application machines, DoNotEnforce, its own identity with Tag Contributor on that group. State the boundary: the Owner tag here is Azure metadata; the EC2 instance's own AWS tags and lifecycle are unchanged.
steps.code:
$TargetId = $Demo.Ec2ArcResourceId
$AssignmentId = $Demo.Ec2PolicyAssignmentId
az resource show --ids $TargetId --query '{id:id,type:type,tags:tags,status:properties.status}' -o json
az policy state list --resource $TargetId --filter "PolicyAssignmentId eq '$AssignmentId'" --query '[].{state:complianceState,time:timestamp,resource:resourceId}' -o table
steps.expected: The EC2 Arc machine (the one whose AWS instance ID the connector demo mapped), no Owner tag, and a NonCompliant row under the AWS-resource-group assignment.
steps.troubleshooting: If the compliance row is missing, the assignment has not evaluated yet: during preparation run az policy state trigger-scan --resource-group $Demo.AwsResourceGroup (it takes minutes); on stage, show the missing tag as the before evidence and say evaluation is pending. If the row says Compliant, the tag was re-applied: check that enforcementMode is DoNotEnforce and reset before delivery (see Reset).
steps.speaker: Say: now an AWS server, onboarded by the connector earlier. Only two things change: the target and the assignment. A second assignment exists because the first is scoped to a different resource group and filters on the Event=cas26 tag, which connector-created machines do not carry. The Owner tag lives on the Azure resource; the EC2 instance's own AWS tags do not change.
steps.attendee: The same governance control applies to an AWS server through its Azure Arc representation; a second assignment is needed only because scope and tag filters differ, not because the mechanism differs.

steps.title: Pass 2 result: remediate the AWS server and verify
steps.body: Run the block: the same remediation, task status, tag readback and compliance check against the EC2 target. Compare the two passes aloud: same definition, same identity model, same evidence, different hosting location and resource group.
steps.code:
$RemediationName = 'cas26-ec2-' + (Get-Date -Format 'yyyyMMddHHmmss')
az policy remediation create --resource $TargetId --policy-assignment $AssignmentId --name $RemediationName --resource-discovery-mode ExistingNonCompliant -o json
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'The operation failed. Stop and follow the recovery instructions.' }
az policy remediation show --resource $TargetId --name $RemediationName --query '{state:provisioningState,deployed:deploymentStatus}' -o json
az resource show --ids $TargetId --query tags -o json
az policy state list --resource $TargetId --filter "PolicyAssignmentId eq '$AssignmentId'" --query '[].{state:complianceState,time:timestamp}' -o table
steps.expected: The remediation task succeeds, the Owner tag is present on the EC2 Arc representation with the governed value, unrelated tags are unchanged, and the next Policy evaluation reports Compliant with a fresh timestamp.
steps.troubleshooting: A remediation failure with an authorization error means the assignment identity lacks Tag Contributor at the AWS resource group: re-run shared/foundation/scripts/Ensure-Cas26AwsArcOwnerTagGovernance.ps1 in plan mode to confirm the grant. A pending compliance row is normal for several minutes; show the tag readback as the resource evidence.
steps.speaker: Say: same policy, same steps, two hosting locations. The tag proves the control works, not that a human accepted ownership. Transition: what the Policy demo proved.
steps.attendee: One procedure governed an on-premises guest and an AWS server. The evidence to keep is the same for both: exact IDs, acting identity, before/after tag, task result and the fresh evaluation timestamp.

demos.title: Update Manager across every estate: assess, schedule, patch, prove
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: most teams patch each estate with its own tool, so nobody can answer 'is everything patched?' in one place. Azure Update Manager works on Azure VMs and Arc-enabled servers alike, so one view, one schedule and one run can cover on-premises and AWS servers. We show it in four steps: one view of pending updates, how a schedule picks machines by tag, one run that patches an on-premises and an AWS test machine together, and proof that it worked.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: ring0-canary is the value of the UpdateRing tag on the first, low-risk machines patched in each cycle (the canaries); the ring0 maintenance configuration is the schedule for them. cas26-arcwin01 is the on-premises canary and iic-cas26-dev-web-01 an AWS dev canary. The IIC workers (including the on-premises worker cas26-lnx01) carry the sample application's orders and are never patched live.

To reproduce: Arc-enabled servers (and, optionally, Azure VMs) with periodic assessment on (the built-in Azure Policy that configures periodic checking for missing system updates does this), a maintenance configuration with a dynamic scope filtered on your own tags, an agreed reboot setting, and Azure CLI with the resource-graph and connectedmachine extensions.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: Update Manager is deployed per the lab update-management design: periodic-assessment policy at the operations and AWS resource groups, five ring maintenance configurations (dev ring0/ring1, prd ring1/ring2, prd SQL) with dynamic scopes, and the UpdateRing/Environment/Workload tags on every CAS26 Arc machine.

Presenter lab: patch canaries only, never the IIC workers or production machines. Confirm both canaries still carry UpdateRing=ring0-canary and appear in the ring0 dynamic scope; if a rehearsal moved one to another ring, put it back before delivery.

Presenter lab: the Azure part of the one view needs an Azure VM with periodic assessment in scope; the lab scopes Update Manager to the Arc machines in the two CAS26 resource groups. Check in rehearsal which Azure VMs appear in Update Manager > Machines and in the step 1 query; if none, say that the same list and query include Azure VMs natively rather than implying one is on screen.

Presenter lab: ServiceUrl in demo.local.json is the IIC order endpoint used by the fresh order in step 5. Set $AwsCanary to the AWS canary's Arc machine name in the presenter terminal before the demo (for example $AwsCanary = 'iic-cas26-dev-web-01').
Rehearse the one-time update so its duration is known; choose security classification only and a reboot setting agreed with the machine owners.
demos.reset: Nothing to reset: this demo changes no tags or schedules. Installed updates stay installed; do not uninstall patches as a reset. Leave the maintenance configurations, dynamic scopes, tags and policy assignments in place, and confirm both canaries are back online after any reboot.
demos.fallback: If a run or assessment is slow, show the rehearsal capture of the one-view query, the ring0 dynamic-scope membership, the one-time run history and fresh assessment for both canary machines, and a fresh order, and name the step you would have run. Never present an unrun patch job as completed.
demos.wait: A one-time update and any reboot take minutes: start it in step 3, explain while it runs, and read the history in step 4. An assessment refreshes a few minutes after a manual trigger; if it has not, use the previous result with its time. The fresh order in step 5 returns immediately.

steps.title: One view: pending updates for Azure, on-premises and AWS machines
steps.body: Open Azure Update Manager > Machines for the CAS26 subscription and show Azure, on-premises and AWS machines in one list with their pending updates. Then load context and run the prepared Resource Graph query: pending critical and security updates per machine (Arc machines and Azure VMs) in the operations and AWS resource groups, with an estate column and each assessment time. One list, one query; where a machine runs is only a column.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
$q = @"
patchassessmentresources
| where type in~ ('microsoft.hybridcompute/machines/patchassessmentresults', 'microsoft.compute/virtualmachines/patchassessmentresults')
| extend rg = tostring(split(id, '/')[4]), machine = tostring(split(id, '/')[8])
| where rg in~ ('$($Demo.OperationsResourceGroup)', '$($Demo.AwsResourceGroup)')
| extend estate = case(type has 'microsoft.compute', 'Azure', rg =~ '$($Demo.AwsResourceGroup)', 'AWS', 'On-premises')
| project estate, machine, rg, os = tostring(properties.osType),
    critical = toint(properties.availablePatchCountByClassification.critical),
    security = toint(properties.availablePatchCountByClassification.security),
    assessedAt = todatetime(properties.lastModifiedDateTime)
| order by estate asc, machine asc
"@
az graph query -q $q --first 50 -o table
steps.expected: One list and one query result show machines from every estate together, each with pending counts and a recent assessment time.
steps.troubleshooting: If a machine is missing, check that it is Arc-connected and in scope of the periodic-assessment policy; say so rather than substituting another machine.
steps.speaker: Step one, one view. Nobody should have to open three tools to answer "is everything patched?": here is every estate in one list and one query, and where a machine runs is just a column.
steps.attendee: One Update Manager view and one Resource Graph query answer "what is pending?" for Azure, on-premises and AWS machines together.

steps.title: How machines get picked: the ring0 schedule and its dynamic scope
steps.body: In Azure Update Manager, open Maintenance configurations and the ring0 dev configuration. Read the window, the classifications and the reboot setting. Then open Dynamic scopes and read the tag filter (Environment and UpdateRing) and the machines it matched from both estates: the on-premises demo machines and the AWS dev machines, none listed by hand.
steps.expected: One schedule selects machines from on-premises and AWS by tag, not by a hand-maintained list.
steps.troubleshooting: If the scope shows no machines, the tags or the scope filter are wrong; show the filter and the machine tags side by side.
steps.speaker: Step two, how machines get picked. The maintenance configuration is the window; the dynamic scope picks machines by tag. A newly onboarded server with the right tags joins this window on its own; nobody edits a machine list.
steps.attendee: A maintenance configuration sets the window; a tag-based dynamic scope decides which machines, from any estate, it patches.

steps.title: Run it: patch one on-premises and one AWS canary in the same window
steps.body: In Update Manager > Machines, select the on-premises canary (cas26-arcwin01) and the AWS dev canary, choose One-time update, tick Security only, set the rehearsed maximum duration and reboot setting, and start it. Explain while it runs; do not wait on screen for a reboot.
steps.expected: A single one-time update is running on one on-premises and one AWS machine.
steps.troubleshooting: If a machine is not eligible (disconnected, unsupported OS or already patched), state the reason from the portal and continue with the other.
steps.speaker: Step three, run it. One run, two estates: an on-premises canary and an AWS canary, patched in the same window. Canaries only: the IIC workers are patched later in their own ring, one estate per window.
steps.attendee: One update run patches machines in different estates in the same window, starting with canaries.

steps.title: Prove it: update history and a fresh assessment for each machine
steps.body: Open Update Manager > History, select the one-time run and read the result, duration and installed updates for each machine. Then run the commands to trigger a fresh assessment on both machines (the first line stops if $AwsCanary is not set) and rerun the step 1 query.
steps.expected: Each machine has a run result and a newer assessment time; pending security counts are lower, or the remaining ones are explained.
steps.troubleshooting: If the assessment has not refreshed yet, show the previous result with its time and say the refresh is still running.
steps.speaker: Step four, prove it. The history proves the run happened; the fresh assessment shows what is still pending on each machine afterwards.
steps.attendee: A completed run and a fresh assessment are different evidence; read both, with their times, for each machine.

steps.title: Prove it: place a fresh IIC order, then debrief
steps.body: Place one demo-tagged IIC order with the shared order client and read its CorrelationId, status and per-stage results: the service still works across Azure, on-premises and AWS. The canaries are not in the order path, so this order shows the service kept working through the window; after the ring2 window that patches the IIC workers, the same order is the recovery proof. Debrief in one sentence, then transition.
steps.code:
if ($Demo.ServiceUrl -match '^PENDING|REPLACE_WITH') { throw 'Populate ServiceUrl in demo.local.json with the IIC order endpoint before delivery.' }
$order = & ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Invoke-Cas26Request.ps1 -BaseUri $Demo.ServiceUrl -DemoTag
$order | Select-Object CorrelationId, OrderNumber, Origin, Status, ElapsedMs
$order.Stages | Format-Table Cloud, Component, Stage, Success, DurationMs
steps.expected: A fresh order completes with every stage answered; the audience can name the schedule, the tag rule, the run result, the fresh assessment and the working service.
steps.troubleshooting: If the order fails or times out, show its stage results and name the stage that failed; do not claim the service is fine. The guard stops the step if ServiceUrl is still a placeholder.
steps.speaker: Debrief: a patch run proves the run; fresh compliance and a working service prove the outcome. Transition: keeping the Kubernetes cluster the way Git says.
steps.attendee: A patch run proves the run; fresh compliance and a working service prove the outcome.

demos.title: Manage the already-onboarded EKS cluster with Flux
demos.objective: What this demo shows and why: with GitOps, Git holds the desired state of a Kubernetes cluster, Flux (running in the cluster) keeps the cluster matching it, and Azure shows whether it matches. We do this on the AWS EKS cluster that the connector onboarded to Arc earlier: point Flux at a reviewed folder in Git and prove that the small ConfigMap it declares really appears in the cluster. AWS still owns the EKS cluster itself; Arc and Flux govern what runs on it.
prerequisites: Names used in this runbook: eks-iic-cas26-use2-01 is the presenter's EKS cluster, Arc-enabled as a connected cluster; cas26-demo is both the Flux configuration name and the Kubernetes namespace reserved for this demo; cas26-operating-contract is the ConfigMap declared in Git (src/sample-service/kubernetes/demo-configmap.yaml).

To reproduce: an Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster with the microsoft.flux extension, a Git repository containing the kustomization folder from this repository, kubectl with a context for the cluster, and Azure CLI with the connectedk8s and k8s-configuration extensions.

Presenter lab: copy config/demo.example.json to config/demo.local.json and fill in the real identifiers (from the CAS26 Key Vault); sign in with az login and select the workload subscription before loading context. Use PowerShell 7 from the repository root. Local validation is not proof that the cloud steps will work.

Presenter lab: verify the EKS account, region and ARN, the matching Arc connectedClusters ID (eks-iic-cas26-use2-01, Connected), the Kubernetes context, the Arc agents, the Flux extension and repository access. Never reconnect an existing Arc cluster.

Presenter lab: reserve Flux configuration cas26-demo and namespace cas26-demo exclusively for this exercise; neither may contain unrelated objects. Review the repository/branch and exact commit before live creation. The manifests include a Namespace plus a ConfigMap, requiring cluster scope.

Presenter lab: preinstall and verify the shared microsoft.flux extension and required CLI extensions. Configure private repository authentication separately without showing credentials. Do not put tokens into demo.local.json or command history.

Presenter lab: use a dedicated reviewed branch that will not change unexpectedly during the session. Review and record its current commit; prune=true can delete owned objects, including the namespace in this repository.
demos.reset: Default is retain for both sessions. For an explicitly scheduled reset, inspect all namespaced resource kinds and ownership first; refuse cleanup if anything unrelated exists or inspection is incomplete. Then delete only Flux configuration cas26-demo with its scoped CLI command and verify pruning of owned objects. Do not separately delete shared flux-system, microsoft.flux, Arc agents or EKS. Preserve the recorded commit and evidence.
demos.fallback: If reconciliation or the portal is slow, show the rehearsal capture of the reviewed commit, the Azure reconciliation state and the in-cluster ConfigMap tied to the EKS ARN/Arc ID/context, and name the step you would have run. A static ConfigMap example is not proof of Flux.
demos.wait: Source fetch and reconciliation run on Flux's interval. Keep the extension and repository access ready, use the existing verified configuration when required, and report pending or error states without repeating create commands.

steps.title: The same EKS cluster, now as an Arc resource
steps.body: Load context, split the Arc cluster ID into its resource group and name, and run the two commands: the Arc cluster's connection state, then the local kubectl context. Compare the EKS ARN noted in the connector demo with the prepared mapping and the kubectl context before running any cluster command.
steps.code:
. ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/scripts/Enter-DemoContext.ps1 -ConfigPath ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/config/demo.local.json
$clusterParts = $Demo.EksArcResourceId.Split('/')
$ClusterRg = $clusterParts[4]
$ClusterName = $clusterParts[8]
az connectedk8s show --resource-group $ClusterRg --name $ClusterName --query '{id:id,connectivity:connectivityStatus,provisioning:provisioningState}' -o json
kubectl config get-contexts $Demo.KubernetesContext
steps.expected: A Microsoft.Kubernetes/connectedClusters resource with connectivity Connected for the intended EKS cluster (not AKS, not a server), and the configured kubectl context listed.
steps.troubleshooting: If the cluster shows Offline or the context is missing, stop: check KubernetesContext and EksArcResourceId in demo.local.json and show the rehearsal capture. Never substitute another cluster.
steps.speaker: Say: remember the EKS cluster from the connector demo; this is how you govern it. AWS still owns the EKS cluster itself; Arc and Flux govern what runs on it.
steps.attendee: Confirm the exact Arc-enabled Kubernetes cluster and kubectl context before any cluster command; the EKS cluster appears in Azure as a connected cluster, not as AKS or a server.

steps.title: Check what is already there
steps.body: Run the four commands: installed cluster extensions, existing Flux configurations, then the cas26-demo namespace and ConfigMap (every kubectl command names the context explicitly). If cas26-demo already exists, it must be proven to belong to this exercise; a matching name alone is not enough.
steps.code:
az k8s-extension list --cluster-name $ClusterName --resource-group $ClusterRg --cluster-type connectedClusters -o table
az k8s-configuration flux list --cluster-name $ClusterName --resource-group $ClusterRg --cluster-type connectedClusters -o table
kubectl --context $Demo.KubernetesContext get namespace cas26-demo --ignore-not-found
kubectl --context $Demo.KubernetesContext get configmap cas26-operating-contract --namespace cas26-demo --ignore-not-found -o yaml
steps.expected: The microsoft.flux extension installed; either no cas26-demo configuration yet or one that points at the reviewed repository; the namespace and ConfigMap absent or clearly owned by this exercise.
steps.troubleshooting: If namespace ownership is uncertain or Flux config points elsewhere, stop. Do not adopt/delete an existing resource or extension to force the exercise.
steps.speaker: Say: before changing a cluster, look at what is already there: the Flux extension, any existing configuration, and the namespace we will use.
steps.attendee: Know what a cluster already runs (extensions, Flux configurations, namespaces) before you add desired state to it.

steps.title: Review exactly what Git will apply
steps.body: Show the two local manifests, then the remote branch's current commit. Local files alone do not prove what the remote branch contains, so record the commit. Explain the Namespace cas26-demo and the ConfigMap cas26-operating-contract with its owner and expected-state keys.
steps.code:
Get-Content ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/src/sample-service/kubernetes/kustomization.yaml
Get-Content ./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/src/sample-service/kubernetes/demo-configmap.yaml
git ls-remote --heads $Demo.FluxRepositoryUrl $Demo.FluxBranch
steps.expected: The remote source is accessible and its branch commit is recorded; the reviewed Git path contains only the intended namespace and ConfigMap.
steps.troubleshooting: If git ls-remote fails, the repository or branch is wrong or not reachable from the jump: check FluxRepositoryUrl and FluxBranch, and show the rehearsal capture. Never point Flux at an unreviewed repository.
steps.speaker: Say: this is the desired state, in Git: one namespace and one small ConfigMap. Anything in this folder will be applied, and removed again if it is deleted from Git.
steps.attendee: Review the exact commit Flux will apply; the remote branch, not your local copy, is the source of truth.

steps.title: Point Flux at the reviewed folder
steps.body: If cas26-demo already exists from rehearsal and matches the reviewed source, skip this command and inspect it in step 5. Otherwise run it: it creates a Flux configuration on the Arc cluster that watches the branch and applies the kustomization folder. Cluster scope is needed because the manifest contains a Namespace; it does not authorize any other repository.
steps.code:
az k8s-configuration flux create --cluster-name $ClusterName --resource-group $ClusterRg --cluster-type connectedClusters --name cas26-demo --namespace flux-system --scope cluster --url $Demo.FluxRepositoryUrl --branch $Demo.FluxBranch --kustomization name=cas26 path=./sessions/hybrid-operations-2026/demos/src/sample-service/kubernetes prune=true
if ($LASTEXITCODE -ne 0) { throw 'The operation failed. Stop and follow the recovery instructions.' }
steps.expected: The CAS26 Flux configuration references only the approved source/path. Configuration creation is not yet proof that objects were applied.
steps.troubleshooting: If the create fails, read the error: repository authentication, Flux extension provisioning or a name clash with an existing configuration. Show the rehearsal capture; never swap in an unreviewed repository or install broader cluster components on stage.
steps.speaker: Say: we tell Azure, and Azure tells Flux in the cluster: watch this folder on this branch and keep the cluster matching it.
steps.attendee: A Flux configuration tells the cluster which repository, branch and folder to follow; creating it is not yet proof that anything was applied.

steps.title: Is the cluster matching Git?
steps.body: Run the commands: the Flux configuration as Azure sees it (compliance state, source revision, kustomization status), then the GitRepository and Kustomization objects inside the cluster. Compare the revision with the commit recorded in step 3; a branch name alone does not prove matching content.
steps.code:
az k8s-configuration flux show --cluster-name $ClusterName --resource-group $ClusterRg --cluster-type connectedClusters --name cas26-demo -o json
kubectl --context $Demo.KubernetesContext get gitrepositories,kustomizations --namespace flux-system -o wide
steps.expected: complianceState Compliant with the source revision equal to the recorded commit, and Ready True for the GitRepository and Kustomization in flux-system; or an explicit pending or error state that is read aloud.
steps.troubleshooting: Azure status can lag in-cluster reconciliation. Inspect controller conditions/events through the scoped configuration rather than declaring success from Succeeded provisioning alone.
steps.speaker: Say: this is Azure showing whether the cluster matches what Git says, at which commit.
steps.attendee: Azure reports whether the cluster matches Git and at which commit; check the revision, not just a green status.

steps.title: See the object in the real cluster
steps.body: Read the ConfigMap from the explicit context and namespace. Compare its data with the file reviewed in step 3. Never kubectl apply the object by hand and then claim Flux reconciled it.
steps.code: kubectl --context $Demo.KubernetesContext get configmap cas26-operating-contract --namespace cas26-demo -o yaml
steps.expected: owner=hybrid-operations, change-boundary=dedicated-demo-namespace and expected-state=reconciled-by-azure-arc-flux match the source, together with successful reconciliation evidence.
steps.troubleshooting: Object presence without revision/controller evidence could be a previous/manual object. Preserve the distinction.
steps.speaker: Say: and here it is in the cluster itself: the ConfigMap Git declared, applied by Flux, not by me.
steps.attendee: Check the object in the cluster itself and compare it with Git; its presence alone could be a leftover or a manual change.

steps.title: Before any cleanup: check what would be deleted
steps.body: Normally leave the configuration in place for the other session. If you are resetting between rehearsals, run the block: it lists every namespaced resource in cas26-demo, of every kind. Because the Git folder includes the Namespace and prune=true is set, deleting the configuration can remove that namespace and everything in it. Stop if anything there is not owned by this exercise.
steps.expected: The reset impact is understood. Shared extension, Arc agents, connector and EKS cluster are never reset by this exercise.
steps.troubleshooting: An enumeration error is an incomplete ownership check, not permission to delete. Do not rely on kubectl get all; it omits resource kinds.
steps.speaker: Say: pruning is powerful: remove it from Git and Flux removes it from the cluster. So before any cleanup, look at everything the namespace holds.
steps.attendee: With prune enabled, removing something from Git removes it from the cluster; check everything a namespace holds before any cleanup.

steps.title: Close with management proof, then Cost
steps.body: Keep the configuration unless a reset was planned and step 7 found only exercise-owned objects; the delete command is kept commented out on purpose. Finish by contrasting connector onboarding (earlier) with Flux desired-state management (now), and name the costs the enabled services add. Transition to section 4, Cost.
steps.code:
# Optional between-rehearsal reset ONLY after the ownership gate:
# az k8s-configuration flux delete --cluster-name $ClusterName --resource-group $ClusterRg --cluster-type connectedClusters --name cas26-demo --yes
# Never delete the shared microsoft.flux extension, Arc agents or EKS cluster.
steps.expected: The audience sees actual management evidence and a bounded cleanup plan, with no claim of taking over EKS lifecycle.
steps.troubleshooting: Nothing runs here. If an earlier step fell back to a capture, name what it would have shown before moving on.
steps.speaker: Show the commit and the resulting ConfigMap together: that is the management result; the connector list was only the prerequisite. Git said how it should look, Flux made it so, Azure shows it matches, and AWS still owns the cluster. Transition to section 4, Cost: what does it cost, and how do we keep it in check?
steps.attendee: GitOps reconciles reviewed desired state into the existing cluster. Repository permissions, namespace ownership and pruning behavior are part of the change boundary.
